Together they show Drift forming and continuing, No Active Drift, Insufficient Evidence, and two Core Values in different states, with verification scope recorded in Appendices B and D. evidence_excerpts.text: Twinkl contributes a deployed, inspectable proof of concept. The evaluations use synthetic Journal Entries, with project-team human annotation for label agreement and AI review of downstream outputs; the benefit to real users remains untested.

The following research questions guide a technical evaluation using synthetic Journal Entries, with human annotation used to assess agreement on a subset of LLM-Judge VIF Labels. Overarching question: To what extent can AI identify and explain divergence between a person's stated values and the behaviour described in their journal writing?

Agreement with human annotators. Three project members independently annotated 115 Journal Entries from 19 of the 204 Personas using an annotation tool as seen in Figure [6](#fig-141). These 19 Personas were selected to give a fair representation of all Schwartz values: each value was a Core Value for at least three Personas, except Stimulation, which had two. Annotators scored all ten values for each Journal Entry as −1, 0 or +1, the same scale the LLM-Judge used. evidence_excerpts.text: Can AI notice when a person's everyday choices move away from their Core Values? Twinkl studies this question as evidence-grounded accountability rather than affirmation, comparing longitudinal Journal Entries with user-confirmed Core Values drawn from Schwartz's Theory of Basic Human Values. Because real journals are private and slow to accumulate, we built a synthetic corpus of 1,651 Journal Entries from 204 Personas and labelled it with an LLM-Judge, after assessing its label agreement with project-team human annotators and its consistency across repeated passes.

Agreement with human annotators. Human--human agreement of 0.56 is \"moderate\" on the Landis and Koch scale \[33\] and indicates annotation difficulty on the shared benchmark: three careful annotators often disagreed about which values a Journal Entry supports or works against. The LLM-Judge agreed with each annotator more closely (0.66) than the annotators agreed with one another; the mean pairwise human--human Cohen's $\kappa$ is also 0.56, so the comparison is like-for-like.

The synthetic corpus provides designed demographic and narrative coverage rather than population representativeness. Generation and original labelling used the same model family, so their errors may be correlated, but this was not measured, and the original generation and labelling procedures could not be reproduced because their model identifiers were not recorded. Human agreement was assessed on only 115 Journal Entries from 19 Personas by three project-team annotators, with just two Personas having Stimulation as a Core Value.
